title: Make Lexicographically Smallest Array by Swapping Elements
summary: Given a 0-indexed array of positive integers nums and a positive integer limit, you can perform an operation any number of times.
statement: Given a 0-indexed array of positive integers nums and a positive integer limit, you can perform an operation any number of times. In one operation, you can choose any two indices i and j such that the absolute difference between nums[i] and nums[j] is less than or equal to limit, and then swap the values at these indices. The task is to return the lexicographically smallest array that can be obtained through these operations. An array a is considered lexicographically smaller than an array b if the first element where they differ satisfies a[i] < b[i].
constraints: nums is nonempty and positive; limit is positive.
Values at any indices may swap when their current absolute difference is at most limit, repeatedly.
Return the lexicographically smallest reachable array.
reference_solution:
def lexicographically_smallest_swappable_array(nums,limit):
    ordered=sorted((value,index) for index,value in enumerate(nums));answer=[0]*len(nums);left=0
    while left<len(nums):
        right=left+1
        while right<len(nums) and ordered[right][0]-ordered[right-1][0]<=limit:right+=1
        indices=sorted(index for _,index in ordered[left:right])
        for index,(value,_) in zip(indices,ordered[left:right]):answer[index]=value
        left=right
    return answer

hints: Swap reachability forms components along consecutive gaps in value-sorted order.
Partition sorted (value,index) pairs wherever a gap exceeds limit; within each component assign smallest values to smallest original indices.
Sort pairs, scan components, sort their indices, and zip them with already-sorted component values.
Adjacent value-chain swaps connect every component permutation, while no operation crosses a larger gap; sorted assignment is therefore the lexicographic minimum independently per component.
